newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Britain's Portillo assures Falklands on security.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Portillo assures Falklands on security.

text.p: British Defense Secretary Michael Portillo said on Thursday Britain would defend the Falkland Islands, its remote South Atlantic outpost, and that it still considers itself a global military power.

"The government's policy on the Falklands ... is the pre-eminent example of our belief that people must be able to choose their own future without fear or oppression," he said in the speech, an advance copy of which was given to news media.
Portillo arrived in the Falkland Islands on Wednesday to reassure their 2,400 residents his government would not weaken the islands' defenses against Argentina.
"The government is committed to defending the islands and maintaining their security. There is no caveat, exception or time limit to that commitment," he said in his speech.
Portillo put Britain's Falklands strategy in the context of a world-wide commitment to stay engaged in military matters, including those in Asia and the Gulf.
Britain has been willing to use troops in international conflicts in the past, as shown in the Gulf and Bosnia, and is willing to do so alone, as in the Falklands, he said.
"The United Kingdom is a major European country, and more than that a power with worldwide vision," he said.

After arriving on a commercial jet from Chile, Portillo said on Wednesday his government was pleased by the conciliatory tone of recent statements by Argentine President Carlos Menem, whose government claims the South Atlantic archipelago.
The British call the islands the Falklands while Argentines call them the Malvinas.
But he rejected Menem's suggestion of the possibility of some kind of shared sovereignty over the islands, saying Britain had nothing further to say on Menem's proposal.
"Britain has always made clear that sovereignty is not only not for sharing and not for surrendering but also not for discussion," he told Reuters.

"I am pleased by the tone of some of the remarks made by President Menem and indeed there has been some important advances in our relations," he said. "(But) British sovereignty in the Falklands is a fact of life. We hope that the Argentines can recognize that."
Argentine forces, acting on a long-standing sovereignty claim, seized the islands in 1982 but were dislodged 10 weeks later by a British task force. Argentina maintains its sovereignty demand.
Any suggestion of Argentine sovereignty makes kelpers, as the islanders are known, bristle.
"No way. Never," said one sheep rancher.
Since the war Britain has reinforced the bare, windswept islands with about 2,000 troops and built a huge military complex and airport on the site of a former sheep ranch.

Islanders, who refer to the day the Argentines capitulated in 1982 as Liberation Day, say they are still nervous about Argentina's intentions despite a British defense buildup that Portillo said cost 3.6 billion pounds since the war.
"Most people are now confident of the British commitment," said the islanders' London-appointed governor, Richard Ralph.

"I don't think people feel they are under military threat. But they don't react well to reiterations by the Argentine government of its intentions to recover sovereignty by the year 2000," Ralph told Reuters.

Once dependent on wool, the islands are now feeling a rare prosperity thanks to the sale of fishing licenses to big foreign trawlers working nearby. Foreign oil companies are due to start full-scale oil exploration in late 1997.
